currentFacts: One of the few large pterosaurs known from the Morrison Formation.
Had a significant bony crest extending to the tip of its snout.
Its wingspan is estimated to have been around 2.5 meters.

name: Mesadactylus
currentFacts: One of the earliest recognized pterodactyloid pterosaurs in North America.
Was quite small, with an estimated wingspan under 1 meter.
Its isolated bones were initially confused with bird remains.

name: Jianchangnathus
currentFacts: Had a highly robust lower jaw with a prominent chin.
Only three teeth were present in each maxilla.
Its tail was relatively straight and rigid.

name: Fenghuangopterus
currentFacts: A member of the scaphognathine group of pterosaurs.
Had a blunt, short skull packed with vertically oriented teeth.
Provides key insights into early pterosaur diversity in Asia.

name: Liopleurodon
currentFacts: A formidable apex predator of the Jurassic seas.
Though famously portrayed as 25 meters long, it actually reached about 6-7 meters.
Had an exceptionally powerful bite force.

name: Plesiosaurus
currentFacts: Characterized by a small head, long neck, and four large flippers.
Moved through the water by flying with its flippers, like modern sea turtles.
Its diet consisted mainly of fish and small cephalopods.

name: Ichthyosaurus
currentFacts: Convergent evolution gave it a body shape strikingly similar to a modern dolphin.
Gave birth to live young at sea, as proven by fossilized mothers with embryos.
Had massive eyes reinforced by bony rings for deep-water vision.

name: Ophthalmosaurus
currentFacts: Had the largest eyes relative to body size of any known vertebrate.
Its enormous eyes suggest it hunted in deep, dark waters.
Possessed a teardrop-shaped body built for high-speed swimming.

name: Cryptoclidus
currentFacts: Had a surprisingly fragile skull for a marine predator.
Its jaws were lined with dozens of interlocking, needle-like teeth.
Likely fed by trapping small fish and soft-bodied squid.

name: Rhomaleosaurus
currentFacts: A large, robust pliosaur with a powerful build.
Had an internal nasal passage that allowed it to smell underwater.
Hunted other large marine reptiles as well as big fish.

name: Macroplata
currentFacts: Had an unusually long neck for an early pliosaur.
Its skull was robust and crocodilian in shape.
Reached about 4.5 meters in length.

name: Peloneustes
currentFacts: A relatively small pliosaur, measuring around 3 meters long.
Had fewer, more robust teeth than its relatives.
Specialized in hunting hard-shelled prey like ammonites and belemnites.

name: Pliosaurus
currentFacts: An enormous apex predator of the Late Jurassic.
Its skull could reach over 2 meters in length.
Its bite force was powerful enough to crush a car.

name: Simolestes
currentFacts: Had a remarkably short, blunt snout.
Its jaw muscles were exceptionally large, giving it a very powerful bite.
Likely specialized in twisting chunks of flesh off large prey.

name: Temnodontosaurus
currentFacts: One of the largest known ichthyosaurs, reaching up to 12 meters.
An apex predator that fed on other marine reptiles and large cephalopods.
Possessed large, robust teeth with distinct cutting edges.

name: Excalibosaurus
currentFacts: Like Eurhinosaurus, it had an extremely elongated upper jaw.
Its front flippers were much shorter than those of its relatives.
Helps document the evolutionary transition of swordfish-like ichthyosaurs.

name: Morganucodon
currentFacts: One of the earliest and most transitional forms between cynodonts and true mammals.
Had a double jaw joint, a hallmark of early mammalian evolution.
Was a tiny, shrew-like animal that hunted insects at night.

name: Castorocauda
currentFacts: The earliest known mammal-like animal with a beaver-like tail and webbed feet.
Provides evidence that early mammaliaforms were highly specialized, not just generalized shrews.
Preserves the oldest known evidence of mammalian hair.

name: Volaticotherium
currentFacts: The earliest known gliding mammal-like animal.
Pushed back the origin of mammalian gliding flight by 70 million years.
Had sharp teeth adapted for a purely insectivorous diet.

name: Fruitafossor
currentFacts: Had remarkably strong forelimbs adapted for digging, like a modern mole or aardvark.
Its tube-like, rootless teeth were perfectly suited for eating colonial insects like termites.
Shows that early mammals were highly ecologically diverse.

name: Juramaia
currentFacts: The earliest known eutherian (placental) mammal.
Pushed back the divergence date of placental and marsupial mammals by 35 million years.
Its forelimbs indicate it was an agile tree climber.

name: Agilodocodon
currentFacts: An early mammaliaform that was highly adapted for living in trees.
Its teeth suggest it had a specialized diet of tree sap.
Possessed highly flexible wrists and elbows for grasping branches.

name: Giganotosaurus
currentFacts: It had highly serrated teeth ideal for slicing flesh.
Possessed an elongated skull with an underdeveloped sense of smell compared to T. rex.
Likely preyed on giant titanosaur sauropods.

name: Deinonychus
currentFacts: Its name means 'terrible claw', referring to the large sickle claw on its foot.
Provided crucial evidence for the evolutionary link between dinosaurs and birds.
Often found in groups, suggesting possible pack-hunting behavior.

name: Albertosaurus
currentFacts: The bonebed discovery suggests it may have lived and hunted in packs.
Was lighter and faster than the closely related Tyrannosaurus rex.
Grew at a rapid pace, reaching mature size in less than 20 years.

name: Utahraptor
currentFacts: The largest known member of the dromaeosaurid family.
Its massive sickle claw could reach up to 9.4 inches in length.
Built for power rather than speed, unlike smaller raptors.

name: Oviraptor
currentFacts: Had a short, parrot-like beak with no teeth.
Likely possessed a crest on its head, similar to a modern cassowary.
Its brooding posture strongly resembles that of modern birds.

name: Majungasaurus
currentFacts: Provides the first unambiguous evidence of dinosaur cannibalism.
Had a distinctive dome on its skull, unique among theropods.
Possessed robust, muscular hind legs but very short arms.

name: Baryonyx
currentFacts: Had a long, narrow snout resembling that of a crocodile.
Its large thumb claw was likely used to hook fish out of water.
Represents one of the earliest known spinosaurid dinosaurs.

name: Acrocanthosaurus
currentFacts: Characterized by tall neural spines along its back and neck.
Likely the apex predator of the Early Cretaceous in North America.
Its tracks have been found alongside those of giant sauropods in Texas.

name: Dromaeosaurus
currentFacts: Had a heavily built skull with a stronger bite force than Velociraptor.
Relied on its jaws rather than its claws to kill prey.
Was one of the first 'raptor' dinosaurs discovered.

name: Troodon
currentFacts: Had one of the largest brain-to-body size ratios of any dinosaur.
Possessed large, forward-facing eyes, suggesting excellent nocturnal vision.
Its serrated teeth suggest an omnivorous diet.

name: Gorgosaurus
currentFacts: Coexisted with another tyrannosaurid, Daspletosaurus.
Had a lighter and more gracile build compared to T. rex.
Possessed a small horn-like crest in front of its eyes.

name: Daspletosaurus
currentFacts: Was heavier and more robust than its contemporary, Gorgosaurus.
Considered by some scientists to be a direct ancestor of Tyrannosaurus rex.
Had proportionally larger teeth than T. rex.

name: Styracosaurus
currentFacts: Characterized by a spectacular frill adorned with up to six long spikes.
Its nose horn could grow up to two feet long.
Despite its fearsome appearance, it was a strict herbivore.

name: Pachyrhinosaurus
currentFacts: Lacked horns on its face, instead having massive bony bosses.
The bosses were likely used in head-butting combat.
Adapted to cold environments, with some fossils found near the Arctic Circle.

name: Centrosaurus
currentFacts: Had a single large horn on its snout and small hornlets on its frill.
Lived in vast herds, potentially numbering in the thousands.
Many died in mass drowning events while crossing flooded rivers.

name: Chasmosaurus
currentFacts: Its frill had massive openings (fenestrae) to reduce weight.
The frill was likely brightly colored for display purposes.
Possessed small brow horns compared to later relatives like Triceratops.

name: Psittacosaurus
currentFacts: Preserved fossils reveal it had long quill-like bristles on its tail.
We know its exact color pattern due to fossilized melanosomes.
It swallowed stones (gastroliths) to help grind up tough plant matter.

name: Pentaceratops
currentFacts: Its name means 'five-horned face', including its two elongated cheek bones.
Has one of the largest skulls of any known land animal.
Lived further south than many of its northern ceratopsian relatives.

name: Diabloceratops
currentFacts: Named for the pair of devil-like horns curving up from the back of its frill.
Had a shorter, deeper snout than most other ceratopsians.
Helped prove that early ceratopsids diversified in southern Laramidia.

name: Kosmoceratops
currentFacts: Possessed 15 distinct horns or horn-like structures on its skull.
Its name translates to 'ornate horned face'.
The frill horns curled completely downward and forward.

name: Zuniceratops
currentFacts: The earliest known ceratopsian to feature true brow horns.
Lacked a solid frill, retaining a lighter, fenestrated structure.
Shows that large brow horns evolved before massive size in ceratopsians.

name: Sinoceratops
currentFacts: Features a frill adorned with forward-curving hornlets.
Lacked brow horns, but had a prominent nasal horn.
Its presence in Asia challenged prior theories of ceratopsid migration.

name: Einiosaurus
currentFacts: Distinctive for a prominent nasal horn that curved forward like a bottle opener.
Its name means 'buffalo lizard' in the Blackfoot language.
Only adults possessed the heavily curved horn; juveniles had straight ones.

name: Achelousaurus
currentFacts: Had bony bosses on its snout and above its eyes instead of sharp horns.
Named after Achelous, a Greek river deity who had a horn torn off.
Fossils show a clear progression of horn loss within its lineage.

name: Nasutoceratops
currentFacts: Featured an unusually short, thick snout.
Possessed curved brow horns that resembled those of modern cattle.
Its deep snout indicates it ate tough, fibrous vegetation.

name: Edmontosaurus
currentFacts: Fossilized 'mummies' show detailed skin impressions and even a fleshy head comb.
Replaced its teeth continuously in a massive dental battery.
Was one of the main prey items for Tyrannosaurus rex.

name: Corythosaurus
currentFacts: Its large, plate-like crest resembled a Corinthian helmet.
The crest was hollow and likely used for vocalization.
Lived alongside a vast diversity of other hadrosaurs.

name: Maiasaura
currentFacts: Provided the first solid evidence that dinosaurs cared for their young.
Hatchlings stayed in the nest and were fed by parents until they grew strong.
Lived in massive nesting colonies, much like modern seabirds.

name: Tsintaosaurus
currentFacts: Early reconstructions gave it a unicorn-like spike pointing directly up.
Recent studies show the crest was actually part of a larger, paddle-like structure.
Was one of the most prominent hadrosaurs in Late Cretaceous Asia.

name: Lambeosaurus
currentFacts: Possessed a bizarre crest shaped like a hatchet with a backward-pointing prong.
Its crest was hollow, serving as a resonating chamber.
Crest shape varied significantly based on age and sex.

name: Ouranosaurus
currentFacts: Characterized by elongated neural spines forming a prominent sail on its back.
Its sail may have been used for thermoregulation or display.
Had a specialized thumb spike and a flattened, duck-like bill.

name: Saurolophus
currentFacts: One of the few dinosaur genera found on multiple continents (North America and Asia).
Had a solid, spike-like crest extending backward from its skull.
Skin impressions suggest a frill running down its back.

name: Olorotitan
currentFacts: Possessed a large, hatchet- or fan-shaped hollow crest.
Had a very long neck with 18 vertebrae, more than most hadrosaurs.
Its discovery proved that lambeosaurines diversified in Asia late in the Cretaceous.

name: Shantungosaurus
currentFacts: The largest known non-sauropod dinosaur, reaching up to 16.6 meters in length.
Its skull alone was over 1.6 meters long.
Lacked a cranial crest despite its immense size.

name: Tenontosaurus
currentFacts: Its tail accounted for nearly two-thirds of its total body length.
Frequently found alongside the teeth and skeletons of the predator Deinonychus.
Maintained a network of strong ossified tendons along its spine and tail.

name: Hypsilophodon
currentFacts: Was a small, highly agile bipedal runner.
Had a specialized beak for snipping off vegetation.
Maintained a stiff tail for balance while running.

name: Thescelosaurus
currentFacts: A specimen dubbed 'Willo' was once thought to contain a fossilized heart.
Had a surprisingly heavy build with robust legs.
Possibly dwelled near rivers and streams.

name: Edmontonia
currentFacts: Edmontonia was one of the largest nodosaurs, heavily armored but lacking a tail club unlike ankylosaurs.
It had large shoulder spikes that may have been used in combat with rivals of its own species.
Its name means "from Edmonton," after the Edmonton Formation in Alberta, Canada.

name: Borealopelta
currentFacts: Borealopelta is the best-preserved ankylosaur ever found — so well preserved its original reddish-brown skin pigmentation (melanin) was identified.
The specimen was found by accident in an Alberta oil sands mine in 2011, and took 6 years to prepare.
It counter-shaded darker on top and lighter on bottom, suggesting it lived in environments with large predators that hunted by sight.

name: Euoplocephalus
currentFacts: Euoplocephalus is the best-known ankylosaur, with over 40 specimens making it one of the most studied armored dinosaurs.
Even its eyelids were armored with bony plates, making it extraordinarily well-protected.
Its massive tail club could swing with enough force to break the leg bones of a large theropod.

name: Sauropelta
currentFacts: Sauropelta was a large nodosaur from Early Cretaceous North America with prominent, forward-pointing shoulder spines.
Unlike ankylosaurs, it lacked a tail club, relying entirely on its body armor and spines for defense.
It is one of the best-known nodosaurs, with several complete or near-complete specimens found in Montana and Wyoming.

name: Nodosaurus
currentFacts: Nodosaurus was one of the first ankylosaurs discovered in North America, found in Wyoming in 1889 by Othniel Charles Marsh.
Its name means "node lizard," referring to the bony nodes studding its skin.
It was a slow-moving herbivore that relied entirely on passive armor for defense, lacking any offensive weapons.

name: Tarchia
currentFacts: Tarchia was the largest and last surviving ankylosaur in Mongolia, with a massive tail club used as a weapon.
Its name means "brainy one" because it had a proportionally large braincase compared to other ankylosaurs.
It lived alongside Tarbosaurus and its armor and club were key defenses against such predators.

name: Polacanthus
currentFacts: Polacanthus was an Early Cretaceous ankylosaur from England, one of the first armored dinosaurs found in Europe.
Its armor included large, keeled spines over the shoulders and a broad pelvic shield of fused osteoderms.
The rear half of the skeleton was found first in 1865 and remained enigmatic for years before additional material was discovered.

name: Gastonia
currentFacts: Gastonia was a heavily armored ankylosaur from Early Cretaceous Utah with elaborate shoulder spines.
It is named after Robert Gaston, who discovered the original specimens.
Gastonia lived alongside the predator Utahraptor and its armor was likely a defense against such large predators.

name: Pachycephalosaurus
currentFacts: Featured a domed skull up to 10 inches thick.
May have used its head for flank-butting or intraspecific combat.
Close relative to Stygimoloch and Dracorex, which might be juvenile forms.

name: Stegoceras
currentFacts: Stegoceras was a small pachycephalosaur with a dome of solid bone up to 2.5 cm thick, used in head-butting behavior.
Analysis of bone microstructure confirms the dome grew through life and was used in physical combat.
It is one of the most common pachycephalosaurs, with dozens of specimens from the Judith River Formation in Alberta.

name: Argentinosaurus
currentFacts: Argentinosaurus may be the largest animal to ever walk the Earth, estimated at 70–80 tonnes and 30–40 meters long.
Each of its back vertebrae was nearly 1.6 meters tall — larger than a grown human.
Discovered in Argentina in 1987, its size is still debated as only fragmentary remains are known.

name: Alamosaurus
currentFacts: Alamosaurus was one of the last sauropods in North America, surviving right up to the K-Pg extinction.
At up to 30 meters long, it may have been one of the largest animals to ever walk North America.
Named after Ojo Alamo, New Mexico, where its fossils were first found.

name: Saltasaurus
currentFacts: Saltasaurus was one of the first sauropods discovered with bony armor (osteoderms) embedded in its skin.
Its discovery challenged the assumption that sauropods were unarmored.
It laid eggs in communal nesting sites, with nests containing up to 25 eggs.

name: Amargasaurus
currentFacts: Amargasaurus had two rows of tall neural spines along its neck, which may have supported a sail or acted as display structures.
It is one of the most distinctive sauropods known, immediately recognizable by its neck ornamentation.
Found in the Amargа formation in Argentina, it lived around 130 million years ago.

name: Dreadnoughtus
currentFacts: Dreadnoughtus is known from one of the most complete gigantic titanosaur skeletons ever found, preserving over 70% of the non-skull skeleton.
Estimated at 65 tonnes and 26 meters long, the specimen was still growing at time of death.
Its name means "fears nothing," a reference to the dreadnought-class battleship.

name: Patagotitan
currentFacts: Patagotitan mayorum may be the largest dinosaur ever described, estimated at 69 tonnes and 37 meters long.
It is known from six individuals found on a single farm in Argentina in 2012, making it one of the most complete giant sauropod records.
Its femur (thigh bone) alone was 2.4 meters long — taller than most humans.

name: Rapetosaurus
currentFacts: Rapetosaurus is one of the most completely known titanosaurs from the Cretaceous of Madagascar.
A juvenile specimen preserved almost the entire skeleton, giving researchers rare insight into titanosaur growth.
Its name means "mischievous giant lizard" in Malagasy.

name: Magyarosaurus
currentFacts: Magyarosaurus was a dwarf titanosaur from Late Cretaceous Romania, only 5–6 meters long due to island dwarfism.
It lived on the Hateg Island and represents one of the best-documented cases of insular dwarfism in dinosaurs.
Named after Magyar (Hungarian), it was discovered in Transylvania in the early 20th century.

name: Tupandactylus
currentFacts: Tupandactylus had one of the most elaborate head crests of any pterosaur, made of both bone and a large soft tissue sail.
Named after Tupã, a Guaraní thunder deity, it was discovered in Early Cretaceous rocks of Brazil.
It had a toothless beak and short neck, suggesting it may have been a fruit or seed eater.

name: Pterodaustro
currentFacts: Pterodaustro had over 1,000 long, fine teeth forming a comb-like filter that it used to strain small crustaceans from water — similar to a flamingo.
Its pink coloration has been proposed based on the carotenoid-rich diet it likely shared with flamingos.
It is the earliest known filter-feeding pterosaur, from Early Cretaceous Argentina.

name: Nyctosaurus
currentFacts: Nyctosaurus had a remarkable antler-like bony crest on its skull, with two prongs in a Y-shape, used for display.
Unlike most pterosaurs, adult Nyctosaurus lost its wing claws, making it more dependent on soaring flight.
It was a highly specialized ocean-going pterosaur, adapted for a life at sea similar to modern albatrosses.

name: Ornithocheirus
currentFacts: Ornithocheirus was a large Cretaceous pterosaur with a wingspan estimated at 4–6 meters and a distinctive crest on its snout.
It was a highly capable flier, likely crossing oceanic distances in search of fish.
Fossils are known from England, Brazil, and Morocco, suggesting a wide range.

name: Anhanguera
currentFacts: Anhanguera was a large pterosaur from Early Cretaceous Brazil with twin, rounded crests on its upper and lower jaws.
Biomechanical analysis shows its jaws were well-suited for snatching fish from the water surface while in flight.
Its name means "old devil" in the Tupi language.

name: Hatzegopteryx
currentFacts: Hatzegopteryx was one of the largest flying animals ever, with a wingspan of 10–12 meters and a skull nearly 3 meters long.
It lived on the Hateg Island and, lacking large predatory dinosaurs there, likely filled the apex predator niche itself.
Recent analysis suggests it had a short, robust neck, making it more suited for terrestrial hunting than previously thought.

name: Azhdarcho
currentFacts: Azhdarcho was a large azhdarchid pterosaur from Late Cretaceous Uzbekistan, related to Quetzalcoatlus.
It gave its name to the Azhdarchidae family, one of the last and largest pterosaur lineages.
Its name comes from "Azhdar," a dragon from Central Asian mythology.

name: Kronosaurus
currentFacts: Kronosaurus was one of the largest pliosaurs, with a skull up to 3 meters long and large, conical teeth for gripping large prey.
Named after Kronos (the Greek Titan), it was a top predator of Early Cretaceous seas around Australia and Colombia.
A famous specimen nicknamed "The Plesiosaur" was controversially reconstructed at Harvard with extra vertebrae.

name: Tylosaurus
currentFacts: Tylosaurus was one of the largest mosasaurs, reaching over 14 meters with a distinctively cylindrical, club-like snout tip.
Fossils of Tylosaurus have been found with the remains of other mosasaurs, fish, birds, and diving birds inside their stomachs.
Named from Greek meaning "knob lizard," it patrolled the Western Interior Seaway of North America.

name: Aristonectes
currentFacts: Aristonectes was a polycotylid plesiosaur with an extremely long neck proportionally, up to 30 neck vertebrae.
It lived in the Late Cretaceous of South America and had many small, interlocking teeth for catching fish.
Its name means "best swimmer" in Greek.

name: Prognathodon
currentFacts: Prognathodon was a large mosasaur with massive, rounded crushing teeth adapted for eating hard-shelled prey like ammonites and turtles.
It could reach 10 meters in length and was one of the largest mosasaurs of the Late Cretaceous.
Fossils have been found in North Africa, Europe, and North America.

name: Platecarpus
currentFacts: Platecarpus was a mosasaur that could reach 7 meters long and had a shark-like tail for fast swimming.
Its name means "flat wrist," referring to its paddle-like limbs adapted for marine life.
Platecarpus had large eyes well-suited for hunting in dim underwater conditions.

name: Dolichorhynchops
currentFacts: Dolichorhynchops was a small polycotylid plesiosaur with a very long neck and small head, unlike most pliosaurs.
It is known from exceptionally complete specimens, including a juvenile, giving insights into plesiosaur growth.
Its name means "long-snouted face."

name: Archelon
currentFacts: Archelon was the largest known turtle that ever lived, reaching 4.6 meters in length and weighing over 2 tonnes.
Unlike modern turtles, it had a leathery shell supported by a bony framework rather than solid bone plates.
Its large, hooked beak was well-suited for crushing jellyfish and soft-bodied prey.

name: Deinosuchus
currentFacts: Deinosuchus was a giant crocodilian up to 12 meters long, capable of preying on large dinosaurs.
Bite marks matching its teeth have been found on hadrosaur and tyrannosaur bones.
Its name means "terrible crocodile." It lived in the Late Cretaceous swamps of eastern North America.

name: Xiphactinus
currentFacts: Xiphactinus was a large predatory fish up to 6 meters long, one of the largest bony fish of the Cretaceous.
A famous specimen preserves a 1.8-meter Gillicus fish inside its stomach, swallowed whole.
Its name means "sword ray," referring to its large, fang-like teeth.

name: Cretoxyrhina
currentFacts: Cretoxyrhina mantelli, known as the "Ginsu shark," was one of the largest sharks of the Cretaceous, reaching 7 meters.
Its serrated, blade-like teeth allowed it to slice through prey, earning its nickname from the Ginsu kitchen knife.
Bite marks matching its teeth have been found on mosasaur, plesiosaur, and large fish fossils.

name: Baculites
currentFacts: Baculites was an ammonite with an unusual straight shell (orthocone) rather than the typical coiled form.
It could grow up to 2 meters long and was an extremely abundant predator in the Western Interior Seaway.
Billions of Baculites fossils have been found in Cretaceous shales, making it one of the best-documented ammonites.

name: Jeletzkytes
currentFacts: Jeletzkytes was an ammonite from the Late Cretaceous Western Interior Seaway of North America.
It is notable for its tightly coiled shell with fine ribbing and tubercles on its surface.
Jeletzkytes is commonly found in the Pierre Shale Formation in the Dakotas.

name: Tusoteuthis
currentFacts: Tusoteuthis was a giant squid-like cephalopod from the Late Cretaceous with tentacles estimated at 2 meters long.
It is known primarily from its hard gladius (internal shell) preserved in marine sediments of the Western Interior Seaway.
It may have preyed on small mosasaurs and was itself likely preyed upon by large mosasaurs.

name: Pikaia gracilens
currentFacts: One of the earliest known primitive chordates, a potential ancestor of all vertebrates.
Possessed a proto-backbone called a notochord.

name: Wiwaxia corrugata
currentFacts: Body covered in scales (sclerites) and long defensive spines.
Crept along the seafloor using a slug-like foot.

name: Bothriolepis canadensis
currentFacts: Most widely distributed placoderm genus in the fossil record.
Had heavily armored pectoral fins that could walk on muddy beds.

name: Eusthenopteron foordi
currentFacts: A famous lobe-finned fish showing the transition from fish to land vertebrates.
Internal fin bones directly correlate to limb bones of tetrapods.

name: Hylonomus lyelli
currentFacts: The earliest known undisputed reptile in Earth's history.
Laid amniotic eggs on dry land, breaking dependency on water.

name: Diplocaulus magnicornis
currentFacts: Had a distinctive boomerang-shaped head created by massive bony horns.
Crescent shape of head may have generated lift when swimming.

name: Estemmenosuchus uralensis
currentFacts: Featured complex bony horns and antlers on its head for display.
Mummified skin impressions suggest glandular, hairless skin.

name: Andrewsarchus mongoliensis
currentFacts: Only known from a single giant skull measuring 83 cm in length.
More closely related to hippos and whales than modern wolves.

name: Uintatherium anceps
currentFacts: Had six distinctive bony knobs (horns) on its flat skull.
Males possessed large, saber-like canine teeth for defense.

name: Paraceratherium transouralicum
currentFacts: The largest land mammal known to have ever lived on Earth.
Had a long neck allowing it to browse canopies up to 8m high.

name: Elasmotherium sibiricum
currentFacts: Popularly known as the Siberian Unicorn due to a massive horn dome on its forehead.
Survived long enough to coexist with early human species.

name: Titanoboa cerrejonensis
currentFacts: The largest, longest, and heaviest snake ever discovered.
Fossils show it lived in a tropical rainforest hotter than today's tropics.

name: Moeritherium lyonsi
currentFacts: An early primitive relative of modern elephants, resembling a small tapir.
Fossil evidence suggests semi-aquatic habits similar to a pygmy hippo.

name: Stygimoloch
currentFacts: Stygimoloch is known for elaborate spikes and horns at the back of its thick skull dome.
Some paleontologists argue Stygimoloch may be a juvenile form of Pachycephalosaurus based on bone remodeling evidence.
Its name means "horned devil from the river of death," a reference to the Hell Creek Formation where it was found.

name: Dracorex
currentFacts: Dracorex hogwartsia has a flat, spike-covered skull unlike typical domed pachycephalosaurs.
Its unusual name was voted by children at a museum and references the Harry Potter fictional school Hogwarts.
Jack Horner proposed Dracorex may be a juvenile Pachycephalosaurus, based on immature bone texture.

name: Rajasaurus narmadensis
currentFacts: Possessed a unique bony horn on its forehead formed by the fusion of its nasal and frontal bones, used potentially for display or head-butting.
Lived in a highly volcanic, lake-dotted floodplain environment that also served as a massive communal nesting ground for various dinosaur species.
Had extremely short, stubby arms and a robust neck, similar to other abelisaurids like Carnotaurus, suggesting it relied on its powerful jaws for hunting.

name: Indosuchus
currentFacts: Had a highly specialized narrow skull roof with frontals and parietals fused, forming a prominent crest.
Coexisted with other abelisaurids like Rajasaurus and Indosaurus, suggesting niche partitioning among Cretaceous Indian carnivores.
Its holotype specimen GSI K27/685 went missing from the GSI collections, making it a subject of taxonomic debate.

name: Vasuki
currentFacts: Estimated to have reached a length of 10.9 to 15.2 meters (36 to 50 feet), rivaling the famous Paleocene Titanoboa for the title of the largest snake ever.
Had a very broad, cylindrical body and a heavy build, indicating it was a slow-moving ambush predator that lived in warm, marshy coastal swamps.
Lived during a period of global warming in the Eocene epoch, where high ambient temperatures enabled coldblooded ectotherms to reach such enormous sizes.

name: Sivatherium
currentFacts: One of the largest ruminant mammals that ever lived, standing over 2.2 meters tall at the shoulder.
Had a short, robust neck and sturdy limbs, differing from modern giraffes, and possessed a massive skull topped with large, palm-like ossicones.
Known to have coexisted with early human ancestors, as depicted in ancient rock art in Sahara regions, surviving until about 10,000 years ago.

name: Stegodon ganesa

Gave live birth at sea (viviparity) as its limbs could no longer support walking on land.
Had smooth skin without armor scales, reducing drag in the water.

name: Megaraptor namunhuaiquii
currentFacts: Its famous 35 cm sickle claw was originally misidentified as a giant foot claw like Velociraptor's.
Head of the enigmatic Megaraptora clade, which dominated South American ecosystems after carcharodontosaurids declined.
Possessed highly pneumatic (air-filled) bones, making it agile for an 8-meter long predator.

name: Maip macrothorax
currentFacts: Named 'Maip' after an evil mythological spirit of the Aonikenk (Tehuelche) people representing cold death.
The largest megaraptoran ever discovered, outsizing Megaraptor and Australovenator.
Had an unusually wide, heavy thoracic cavity ('macrothorax') housing large lung systems for high metabolism.

name: Lythronax argestes
currentFacts: Nickname 'Gore King' comes from its scientific name translating directly to 'King of Gore'.
Possessed broad skull rear and narrow snout, giving it overlapping 3D binocular vision like T. rex 13 million years earlier.
Proved that tyrannosaurid radiation occurred much earlier than previously assumed.

name: Moros intrepidus
currentFacts: Filled the 70-million-year gap in North American tyrannosaur evolution.
Existed as a small, nimble predator when giant allosauroids (like Siats) were apex predators.
Extremely long leg bones indicate superior running speed and cursorial agility.

name: Sauroposeidon proteles
geographicRange: {"continent":"North America","region":"Gulf Coast / Interior Plains","country":"United States","fossilFormation":"Antlers Formation, Cloverly Formation"}
currentFacts: Its neck reached up to 12 meters (39 feet) in length, accounting for over one-third of its total body length.
Cervical vertebrae were up to 1.4 meters long and filled with honeycombed internal air cells (trabecular bone).
Stood as tall as a 6-story building, allowing it to browse vegetation inaccessible to any other creature.

name: Psephoderma alpinum
currentFacts: Superficially resembled a marine turtle but belonged to the extinct placodont order of sauropterygians.
Had two distinct protective carapace shields: one covering the shoulders/chest and a smaller one over the pelvis.
Possessed toothless, narrow beaked jaws lined internally with flat, pavement-like crushing plates.

name: Vayuraptor agriculturalis
currentFacts: Coexisted with another medium-sized theropod, Siamraptor, in Early Cretaceous Thailand.
Ankle bones (astragalus and calcaneum) were fused together, enhancing biomechanical sprinting stability.
Species name 'agriculturalis' honors local farmers who assisted in uncovering the fossil site.

name: Rhizodus hibberti
currentFacts: Possessed enormous 22 cm (9 inch) tusk-like teeth anchored deeply into massive jaws.
Could likely lung onto land or shallow swamp margins to snatch terrestrial amphibians, similar to modern crocodiles.
Its skin was covered in heavy, overlapping cosmoid scales providing armor against rival aquatic predators.

name: Gillicus arcuatus
geographicRange: {"continent":"North America","region":"Western Interior Seaway","country":"United States","fossilFormation":"Smoky Hill Chalk"}
currentFacts: Best known as the swallowed prey in the famous 14-foot Xiphactinus specimen at Hays, Kansas.
Possessed numerous fine, needle-like gill rakers used to strain small marine organisms from sea water.
Had deeply embedded, thin circular scales that reduced turbulence during swift schooling swims.

name: Yutyrannus huali
currentFacts: Holds the record as the largest direct feather-bearing animal in Earth's history (9 meters long, 1.4 tonnes).
Feathers were 20 cm long filamentous proto-feathers providing insulation in Liaoning's chilly 10°C climate.
Possessed a high median crest along its snout used for species display and intra-species communication.

name: Nanotyrannus lancensis
currentFacts: Subject of one of the longest and most fiercely contested debates in paleontology history.
Had significantly more teeth (up to 36 in upper jaw) and larger forelimbs than adult T. rex.
Possessed extremely long, slender leg bones adapted for high-speed pursuit running.

name: Palaeoloxodon antiquus
geographicRange: {"continent":"Europe, Asia","region":"Mediterranean & Central Europe","country":"Germany, United Kingdom, Italy, Greece","fossilFormation":"Ebbsfleet Valley deposits"}
currentFacts: One of the largest terrestrial mammals to ever walk the Earth, outsizing the Woolly Mammoth.
Possessed long, nearly straight tusks reaching up to 3.8 meters in length.
Coexisted with Neanderthals and early Homo sapiens, who actively hunted these leviathans with wooden spears.

name: Gryposuchus colombianus
geographicRange: {"continent":"South America","region":"Amazon & Orinoco Basins","country":"Colombia, Venezuela, Brazil","fossilFormation":"La Venta Formation, Urumaco Formation"}
currentFacts: Possessed an extremely elongated, narrow snout packed with over 80 inter-locking needle teeth.
Inhabited the mega-wetlands of Miocene South America alongside giant caimans like Purussaurus.
The hook-like curvature at the tip of its snout helped hold onto slippery, armor-plated prehistoric catfish.

name: Plesiosuchus manselii
currentFacts: The largest metriorhynchid crocodilian ever discovered, outgrowing Geosaurus and Metriorhynchus.
Had wide-opening jaws with coarse serrations adapted for severing flesh from large marine vertebrates.
Shared marine habitats with Dakosaurus, dividing ecological niches based on skull mechanics.

name: Suchodus durobrivensis
geographicRange: {"continent":"Europe","region":"Oxford Clay Basin","country":"United Kingdom, France","fossilFormation":"Oxford Clay Formation"}
currentFacts: Possessed significantly shorter, stronger jaws than Metriorhynchus for crushing armored prey.
Equipped with paddle-shaped limbs and a tail fin for pelagic sea life.
Fossilized eye rings (sclerotic rings) show adaptations for deep diving.

name: Edestus heinrichi
geographicRange: {"continent":"North America, Europe","region":"Illinois Basin","country":"United States, Russia","fossilFormation":"Carbondale Formation"}
currentFacts: Did not shed worn teeth; new teeth grew in from the back, pushing old teeth forward into protruding curved brackets.
Jaws operated like a pair of hedge trimmers, thrashing up and down to slash prey.
Belonged to Eugeneodontida, closely related to modern chimaeras rather than true sharks.

name: Pyroraptor olympius
currentFacts: Named 'Fire Thief' because its fossils were uncovered immediately after a major forest fire.
Possessed a curved 6.5 cm sickle claw on the second toe of each foot for gripping prey.
Fully covered in feathers with wing-like plumage along its forelimbs.

name: Dracovenator regenti
currentFacts: One of the earliest apex theropod dinosaurs discovered in southern Africa.
Possessed paired bony crests running along the top of its skull.
Targeted abundant early sauropodomorph dinosaurs as primary prey.

name: Sarcosaurus woodi
currentFacts: One of the earliest true Jurassic theropod dinosaurs discovered in the UK.
Possessed a small nasal horn or crest similar to Ceratosaurus.
Inhabited coastal mudflats alongside early marine reptiles.

name: Animantarx ramaljonesi
currentFacts: First dinosaur discovered exclusively via radiological radiation detection technology.
Possessed a heavily armored skull with small horn-like projections behind the eyes.
Lacked a tail club, relying instead on shoulder spikes and fused armor plates.

name: Segnosaurus galbinensis
currentFacts: Bizarre theropod that evolved away from meat-eating to become a strict herbivore.
Possessed a massive pot belly to ferment tough plant vegetation.
Equipped with elongated, curved hand claws used to pull down tree branches.

name: Bajadasaurus pronuspinax
currentFacts: Possessed extremely long, thin neural spines along its neck that curved forward over its head.
The neck spines were likely covered in keratin sheaths, acting as defensive spikes against predators while grazing.
Eyes were positioned high on its skull, allowing it to look out for predators while lowering its snout to eat.

name: Fukuiraptor kitadaniensis
currentFacts: Initially thought to be a dromaeosaurid due to a large hand claw, later recognized as a megaraptoran.
The state dinosaur mascot of Fukui Prefecture, Japan.
Possessed large hand claws used to grasp prey.

name: Fukuisaurus tetoriensis
currentFacts: Skull lacked the kinetic flexibility seen in advanced hadrosaurs, chewing with a rigid maxilla.
Coexisted with Fukuiraptor, Fukuititan, and Koshisaurus in Early Cretaceous Japan.
Equipped with a sharp beak for clipping tough vegetation.

name: Leedsichthys problematicus
geographicRange: {"continent":"Europe, South America","region":"Tethys / Boreal Oceans","country":"United Kingdom, France, Germany, Chile","fossilFormation":"Oxford Clay Formation"}
currentFacts: Holds the record as the largest bony fish in Earth's history, rivaling modern baleen whales in ecological role.
Possessed over 40,000 delicate mesh-like gill raker teeth to filter microscopic plankton.
Bite marks on Leedsichthys fins show it was hunted by giant marine predators like Liopleurodon and Metriorhynchus.

name: Suchomimus tenerensis
currentFacts: Possessed a narrow 1.2-meter long crocodile-like skull lined with 100 conical teeth.
Had a massive 30 cm sickle claw on its thumb used to spear fish.
Featured a low neural spine sail reaching up to 60 cm high along its back.

name: Oxalaia quilombensis
currentFacts: Named after Oxalá, the principal deity in the Afro-Brazilian Candomblé pantheon.
The largest carnivorous dinosaur recorded from Brazil.
Close relative of North African Spinosaurus, featuring double functional replacement teeth.

name: Tropaeognathus mesembrinus
currentFacts: One of the largest pre-azhdarchid flying reptiles known, with an 8.2-meter wingspan.
Possessed large convex keel-like crests on the tips of both upper and lower jaws.
Crests acted as rudders to stabilize jaws while dipping into water at high speed to catch fish.

name: Coloborhynchus clavirostris
currentFacts: Featured a unique flattened front snout tip with teeth projecting forward at odd angles.
Equipped with a prominent crest along the front upper jaw.
Earliest recognized anhanguerid pterosaur in the European fossil record.

name: Arctodus simus
geographicRange: {"continent":"North America","region":"Great Plains & Coastlines","country":"United States, Canada, Mexico","fossilFormation":"Rancho La Brea tar pits, Riverbluff Cave"}
currentFacts: Stood over 3.4 meters (11 feet) tall on its hind legs, making it the largest terrestrial mammalian carnivore in North America.
Used its massive size to bully smaller predators like saber-toothed cats (Smilodon) away from fresh kills.
Possessed unusually long, slender legs allowing it to pace efficiently across vast distances.

name: Purussaurus brasiliensis
geographicRange: {"continent":"South America","region":"Amazon Basin","country":"Brazil, Peru, Venezuela","fossilFormation":"Solimões Formation, Urumaco Formation"}
currentFacts: Possessed one of the strongest bite forces of any animal in Earth's history (~69,000 Newtons / 7 tonnes force).
Its massive skull measured 1.4 meters long and was immensely broad for crushing thick mammalian bones.
Consumed over 40 kilograms of meat per day to maintain its giant metabolic needs.

name: Josephoartigasia monesi
geographicRange: {"continent":"South America","region":"Rio de la Plata Basin","country":"Uruguay","fossilFormation":"San José Formation"}
currentFacts: Holds the Guinness World Record as the largest rodent to ever exist on Earth.
Possessed enormous 30 cm incisors with a bite force equivalent to a tiger, used for digging or defense.
Replaced traditional ungulate herbivore niches in prehistoric South American river estuaries.

name: Livyatan melvillei
currentFacts: Possessed the largest functional biting teeth of any known animal in Earth's history (36 cm long and 12 cm wide).
Unlike modern sperm whales which feed on squid using toothless upper jaws, Livyatan had huge teeth in BOTH upper and lower jaws.
Coexisted and directly competed with Megalodon for marine mammalian prey in Miocene oceans.

name: Kelenken guillermoi
currentFacts: Possessed the largest head of any known bird in history, with a skull measuring 71.6 cm (28 inches) long.
Could sprint at estimated speeds exceeding 45 km/h to run down prehistoric mammals.
Killed prey by striking downwards with its massive eagle-like hooked beak like an axe.

name: Varanus priscus
currentFacts: The largest terrestrial venomous squamate reptile in Earth's history.
Possessed venom glands in its lower jaws similar to its smaller living relative, the Komodo Dragon.
Serrated recumbent teeth allowed it to tear open heavy hide of giant extinct marsupials.

name: Daeodon shoshonensis
geographicRange: {"continent":"North America","region":"Great Plains","country":"United States","fossilFormation":"Arikaree Group (Agate Fossil Beds)"}
currentFacts: Nicknamed the 'Hell Pig', though genetically closer to hippos and whales than true pigs.
Possessed a massive 90 cm (3 foot) skull with heavy bony cheek flanges (jugal flanges) for muscle attachment.
Heavily worn teeth show it routinely cracked open giant animal bones to extract nutrient-rich marrow.
